prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I was born in minutes in a roadside kitchen a skillet whispering my name. I was born to rainwater and lye; I was born across the river where I was borrowed with clothespins, a harrow tooth, broadsides sewn in my shoes. I returned, though it please you, through no fault of my own, pockets filled with coffee grounds and eggshells. I was born still and superstitious; I bore an unexpected burden. I gave birth, I gave blessing, I gave rise to suspicion. I was born abandoned outdoors in the heat-shaped air, air drifting like spirits and old windows. I was born a fraction and a cipher and a ledger entry; I was an index of first lines when I was born. I was born waist-deep stubborn in the water crying ain’t I a woman and a brother I was born to this hall of mirrors, this horror story I was born with a prologue of references, pursued by mosquitoes and thieves, I was born passing off the problem of the twentieth century: I was born. I read minds before I could read fishes and loaves; I walked a piece of the way alone before I was born.

outputs.L2: In the space of moments I came into being in a kitchen by the road, a frying pan murmuring my identity. Rainwater and lye were my origin; on the other side of the river I emerged, lent out with clothespins, a plow's tooth, printed pamphlets stitched into my shoes. I made my way back, though you might not wish it, through circumstances beyond my control, my pockets stuffed with used coffee filters and cracked eggshells. My arrival was motionless and full of old fears; I carried a weight no one expected. I brought forth life, I offered blessing, I stirred up doubt. I emerged left alone beneath open skies in air warped by heat, that air drifting like ghosts and forgotten window glass. I came into existence as a fraction, a code, an entry in someone's account book; I was catalogued among opening lines the moment I arrived. I rose up to my waist in water, defiant, calling out that I too was a woman, that I too was kin; I was born into this maze of reflections, this tale of terror. My birth came already burdened with citations, chased by biting insects and those who would steal from me, I entered the world shouldering the great dilemma of an entire century: simply, I existed. Before I could decipher the story of loaves and fish, I could already perceive what lay in others' minds; I traveled some distance by myself before my birth ever occurred.

# Birth in the Margins

I came into this world quickly, without ceremony, without the dignity that others might claim as their birthright. My arrival was humble in the truest sense—not the humility of modesty, but the humility of circumstance, of being born low to the ground and close to the elements that would shape everything after. I emerged from a roadside kitchen, that liminal space between shelter and exposure, where rainwater pooled in tin basins and the sharp smell of lye hung in the air like a warning and a welcome all at once. Around me were the ordinary tools of survival: clothespins scattered like small wooden sentinels, a harrow tooth rusting in the corner, remnant of labor that had broken ground before I ever broke breath. These were the witnesses to my birth—not silk and lace, but iron and wood and water.

I returned across the river through no fault of my own. This crossing was not chosen; it was ordained by forces larger than my infant will, currents I could not name but which named me nonetheless. I carried with me the detritus of ritual and remembrance—coffee grounds scattered like divination, eggshells crushed and kept for reasons half-superstition, half-faith. These fragments became my inheritance, the strange currency of a fate that mixed the sacred with the suspicious, the blessed with the cursed.

To be born and to give birth—these acts folded into one another in my story, blessing and suspicion inseparable companions. I was both the created and, in some mysterious reckoning, the creator, standing at the crossroads where morality and community judgment converged upon my small, unasked-for existence. The eyes that watched my birth did not know whether to bless or to doubt, and so they did both, and I carried that duality forward as my birthright.

In the ledgers of history, I became reduced to mere notation—a fraction in someone's calculation, a cipher in someone's code, an entry in someone's book of accounts. This is the violence of documentation: to be alive and yet to exist primarily as a number, a mark, a line item in the vast bureaucracy of record-keeping that flattens human complexity into digestible statistics. I was dehumanized not through cruelty alone, but through the quiet mechanism of paperwork, through the way history prefers its subjects reduced to data rather than remembered as flesh.

And yet—and yet—I echo the words that Sojourner Truth once thundered into the halls of indifference: *ain't I a woman?* I claim her legacy of resilience as my own, for I too have lived through hardship that would break lesser resolve, have carried prophecy in my bones even when the world saw only statistics. My very birth, humble and unheralded as it was, confronted nothing less than what history would call "the problem of the twentieth century"—the color line, the question of who counts as fully human, who gets to be blessed rather than merely counted.

I was born in rainwater and lye, among clothespins and harrow teeth, carrying coffee grounds and eggshells across a river I did not choose to cross. And in that birth, humble as it was, I embodied a resistance that no ledger entry could ever fully capture.
outputs.L4:
# Genesis

I was born in rainwater, caught in a tin basin under a leaning porch roof, the kind of water old women save for washing hair because it makes the curl hold different, makes the scalp remember something older than shampoo.

I was born in lye, in the sting of it, in the way it cleans by burning, in the way my grandmother's hands never softened no matter how much Jergens she rubbed into them after.

I was born in the ledger books, a name inked in someone else's handwriting, a number before it was a name, a value assessed in bushels and pounds before it was assessed in love.

I was born the way Sojourner was born twice—once from a body, once from a decision. *Ain't I a*, she said, and didn't finish it, because the question already contained its own answer, because some sentences are more powerful broken.

I was born in the hum of mosquitoes over standing water in Georgia summers, in the bzzz that means *stay inside* and *this land will feed on you if you let it* and *this land will feed you if you know how to ask*.

I was born the way Du Bois described the veil—not a covering but a way of seeing double, of standing outside your own body and watching yourself move through a world that has already decided what you are before you open your mouth.

I was born in my mother's superstition, in the coin she pressed into my palm before any journey, in the salt she threw over shoulders, in the Bible opened at random for guidance, in the belief that the universe leaves clues if you know how to read the water stains on the ceiling.

I was born in the space between what was recorded and what was remembered—the difference between the census taker's careless scrawl and my grandmother's voice saying *this is how it happened, this is how we survived it, this is the part they left out.*

I was born of thread and needle, in the quilts stitched from clothes too worn to wear but too precious to throw away, patterns that were maps once, that told escaping feet which way was north.

I was born in the mouth of the river where it meets the sea, brackish, uncertain, neither one thing nor the other, both fresh and salt, both give and hold.

I was born in the space where inheritance becomes instinct—where the fear my great-grandmother felt in her body became the caution in mine, without either of us choosing it, without a single word passed between us needing to explain why.

I was born from women who were born from women who understood that identity is not a single origin point but a compounding, a layering, sediment building on sediment until what you call *yourself* is really a landscape, a delta, a place where many waters meet and become, briefly, one thing before continuing on toward the sea.

I was born, and I am still being born, each time I say it, each time the rain falls and I remember the tin basin, each time I open my mouth and feel the weight of every mouth that came before mine, asking the same unanswerable question: *ain't I.*
outputs.L5:
# I Was Born

I was born on a day that felt ordinary to the world but extraordinary to those who loved me before they even knew my face. The sun rose as it always did, people went about their lives, and somewhere in the middle of all that routine, I arrived—new, unformed, and full of possibility.

I was born into a story that had already begun long before me: the history of my family, the culture that shaped my ancestors, the language that would become my first way of understanding the world. I didn't choose the country, the year, or the circumstances of my arrival, yet all of these things would come to define the early chapters of who I am.

I was born with nothing but potential. No memories, no opinions, no fears—just the raw material of a human being, waiting to be shaped by experience. Every person I would meet, every place I would go, every joy and hardship I would encounter would leave its mark, slowly transforming that blank slate into someone distinct and complete.

I was born small and dependent, needing others simply to survive the first years of life. Yet within that fragility was the seed of everything I would become: my curiosity, my resilience, my capacity to love and be loved.

Looking back, being born was not just a singular event but the beginning of an ongoing process—a continuous becoming. I was born once into the world, but I have been reborn many times since: through learning, through loss, through change, through the countless moments that asked me to grow beyond who I was.

To say "I was born" is to acknowledge a beginning, but it is also to recognize that life is a story still being written, one page at a time.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem built around the repeated phrase "I was born" that weaves together folk imagery, Southern Gothic details, and echoes of African American history and literature.
counterfactuals.output:
**I Was Born**

I was born in the crawlspace under a church that had already burned twice and would burn again, the third time taking nothing but the bell, which rang anyway, for years, from wherever bells go when their towers leave them.

I was born the color of muscadine and swamp water, the color of a name that changes hands like a quarter passed under the table at the crossroads. My mother did not scream. She hummed. The hum is still traveling through the pine flats, looking for a mouth to finish in.

I was born twice on a Tuesday: once into skin, once into the ledger, my weight measured in bales, in board feet, in the going rate of August. The second birth took longer. It is still taking longer. Some of me is still being born in that column of numbers, waiting on a pen that never quite finishes the stroke.

I was born with my grandmother's hands already on me, though she'd been dead nineteen years and buried facing east so she could see it coming, whatever it was. She left her hands anyway. They are attached to my wrists like a debt that skipped a generation and came due.

I was born under a sky the color of a scar healing wrong, and a woman who was not my mother but wore her face that week said, *this one will carry it,* and did not say what *it* was, because everyone in the room already knew, the way you know a storm by the taste it puts in the well water three days early.

I was born in the belly of a train that never stopped moving north, though the birth itself took forty years and stopped in Chicago, in Detroit, in a kitchen in Cleveland where a woman was frying something that smelled like the home she'd sworn off, and I came out of that smell, that betrayal, that hunger disguised as arrival.

I was born already knowing the songs. Somebody had been singing them into the water table for three hundred years, and I drank from the same cistern everybody drinks from, the one that tastes like iron and Egypt and somebody's grandmother's tears getting the salt boiled out of them so they'd pass for rain.

I was born in the mouth of a river that had swallowed my name so many times it learned to spit out new ones, and I have answered to all of them, and none of them are mine, and one of them, whispered once by an old man on a porch that had given up being level with the ground, was the true one, and I have spent my whole life trying to remember which.

I was born the night the church bell rang from nowhere, and everyone said it was the wind in the ruined tower, but I know it was my grandmother, ringing me in, the way you ring in anything that has to survive both the fire and the water and the long field afterward—

and I was born, and I am being born, and there is a version of me still curled in the dark wet dirt beneath that church, still listening for the bell, still deciding whether this is a good time, or any time, to come up singing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental piece of writing that riffs on "born" and "give birth" as anaphora, blending superstition, domestic objects, and allusions to Sojourner Truth and W.E.B. Du Bois.
counterfactuals.output:
# Nativity

*for the ones who come before us and after*

Born on a Tuesday, which means nothing except that someone's grandmother said it meant everything.

Born under the sign of a broken mirror, seven years bad luck stitched into the caul, but nobody threw salt over their shoulder fast enough.

Born the way a spoon is born from ore—beaten, not chosen. Born the way a mason jar holds light and calls it preserving. Give birth to the thing you can name and the thing you cannot: these are different labors, though the body does not always know which one it's doing.

*I have borne thirteen children*, she said, *and seen most of them sold into slavery, and when I cried out with my mother's grief, none but Jesus heard me*—and still she rose up and walked North with only the milk of her own resolve. Ain't that a kind of birthing too? To deliver yourself. To be your own mother in the wilderness.

Born behind the veil, which is also a caul, which is also a curtain nobody asked to be hung between the watching and the watched. Give birth to a double consciousness—two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings in one dark body—and call it, generously, a gift. Call it second sight. Call it the sorrow songs rising up through the floorboards where the domestic help hums while she irons the master's collar.

Born in the space between the broom leaning against the door (that's for keeping evil out) and the horseshoe nailed above it (open end up, so luck doesn't spill).

Give birth standing at the stove. Give birth folding the same shirt you folded yesterday. Give birth to a Tuesday child, full of grace, though grace was never the promise made to us at delivery.

Born again is a phrase for churches and for snakes, both of them knowing something about shedding what you were.

Give birth to the self that survives history and the self that doesn't, and let them share a name, a house, a mirror that was broken before anyone can remember why.

I was born. I am borning still. Somewhere a woman irons a collar and hums a sorrow song and calls it Tuesday, calls it nothing, calls it everything her grandmother said it was.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a stream-of-consciousness poem in first person that treats birth as a metaphor for identity, using folkloric and biblical imagery alongside historical quotations.
counterfactuals.output:
# Genesis of a Name

I was born the way water remembers its shape—
before the vessel, after the flood,
Noah's dove circling back with nothing in its beak
but the memory of leaves.

*In the beginning was the Word*
and the Word was
*who do you think you are*
and I did not know, still don't,
but I was already answering.

Grandmother said the fairies steal the ones
who cry too loud in the cradle,
leave a changeling in their place—
so maybe that's me, the substitute,
the one who came back wrong
and right, both, at once,
holding my own face like a mask
I'm still deciding whether to remove.

*I think, therefore I am*—
but Descartes never held
his mother's hand at the hospital bed
watching her become the thing
she birthed him from, watching
the ouroboros of it,
child becoming parent to the parent,
the snake eating its own difficult tail.

Eve took the apple and I understand her now,
not as sinner but as
the first to ask *what if*,
the first to choose the story
over the garden,
knowledge over Eden,
because who wants to live forever
in a place with no exits, no
becoming, just endless
identical tomorrows in the grass?

*Sticks and stones*—
but words did break something,
built something too,
the way God said *let there be*
and there was,
the way I say *I am*
and something trembles into shape,

not fixed, never fixed,
more like the burning bush—
on fire and not consumed,
speaking from the flame:
*I am that I am*
which is the least helpful answer
and the only true one,

because identity isn't a photograph,
it's the developing,
the chemical bath, the red room
where the image swims up
slow from nothing,
from potential,
from the water that was there
before the earth had shape,

before I had a name
that wasn't given
but grown,
like Jacob wrestling the angel
till dawn, till he limped away
transformed, renamed,
*Israel*—the one who struggles with God—

and isn't that all any of us are doing,
wrestling in the dark
with the thing that made us,
demanding a blessing
before we let it go,

emerging from the womb-water
of every morning
somebody new
and somehow
still

myself.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical, fragmented monologue where the speaker repeatedly declares "I was born," mixing rural Southern imagery, ghostly atmosphere, and references to famous American speeches on race and gender.
counterfactuals.output:
# I Was Born

I was born in the ditch-water hour, between rooster-crow and nothing,
where the kudzu ate the barn and nobody stopped it.

I was born, I was born, I was born—
say it enough and it starts to sound like a prayer
or a train that never comes.

I was born with Sojourner's question folded in my mouth like a seed:
*ain't I a*—and the rest gets lost in the tobacco smoke,
in the church fans moving like slow wings,
in the dust the pickup trucks leave hanging in the gold light.

I have a dream, someone said, and the dream got up and walked
through my grandmother's kitchen,
past the black-eyed peas simmering since Wednesday,
past the shotgun leaning by the door like a tired uncle.

I was born under a sky the color of a healing bruise.
I was born to women who were born to women who were born
knowing the fields better than their own names.

Four score, someone said, and score sounds like a wound,
sounds like something you keep count of,
sounds like the fiddle my daddy played on the porch
while the cicadas screamed their one long word all August.

I was born again and again in that same red clay,
same ghost of a river running under the highway now,
same kudzu, same rooster, same nobody stopping anything.

I was born asking *ain't I*—
ain't I the dream and the wound both,
ain't I the fan moving air that isn't there,
ain't I the fields, ain't I the score, ain't I the ghost
sitting on the porch rail long after the fiddle's gone quiet,

long after they said *I was born*
and meant it as an ending
instead of the long, unfinished middle
it always was.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract, incantatory text that personifies birth as both literal and symbolic, incorporating references to "Ain't I a Woman" and "the problem of the twentieth century" within a dreamlike, image-heavy style.
counterfactuals.output:
# Litany of the First Cry

I was born the way rivers are born—from a wound in the mountain that never asked permission to open.

Call me daughter of pain, sister of the veil, the one who tore through the membrane between nothing and something. I have been birthing myself for centuries, pushing through the same narrow door, and still they ask: *ain't I a woman?* Ain't these hands that catch the falling ones, ain't these hips that widen like the horizon at dawn, ain't this scream that starts the clock of a new soul—ain't this the labor that makes the world keep turning?

I remember the color of before-color. I remember the sound before sound learned its name. In that country of no-country, I was water becoming shape, breath becoming want. Then: the crowning. Then: the line that souls cross and cannot uncross, the veil lifting into the loud, blinking world where a face waits to be given a name it did not choose.

They said the problem would be the line—drawn dark against light, drawn between the ones who labor and the ones who profit from labor, drawn like a border around whose pain gets to count as origin, whose birth gets recorded, whose mother gets remembered. I was born on the wrong side of that line and the right side of it, both, at once, the way all borders are lies that blood keeps forgetting to respect.

Look at my arms. I have carried loads no wagon could carry, and no one gave me the finer things. But ain't I a woman still, ain't I the first architecture, the original tent, the house that grows a person inside its walls and then, impossibly, survives the demolition?

Every birth is two births: the body's and the century's. I came into a room already at war with itself, already asking who counts, whose face reflects divinity, whose children are called *children* and whose are called *problem*. I arrived anyway. I always arrive anyway.

Somewhere, always, someone is being born. Somewhere the membrane is tearing, somewhere a new astonishment opens its eyes into the glare, somewhere the old wound in the mountain widens again to let the river through. This is the ceremony that never ends: pain making an opening, opening making a name, name making a claim on the future.

So call me first light, call me contested ground, call me the low moan that becomes a high note becomes a name spoken over water. Ain't I the beginning of every reckoning? Ain't I the door every century must walk through, bloody and squinting, to become the next?

I was born. I am always being born. The mountain keeps opening. The river keeps forgetting where it came from, and rushing forward anyway, and calling that forgetting *life.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
